UROLOGY__Urinary Tract Infection (UTI):
Overview

Infection of the urinary tract. The decisive fork is lower (cystitis) vs upper (pyelonephritis) -- same organisms, very different severity. Lower UTI can ascend to cause pyelonephritis with sepsis and scarring risk.

Lower UTI (cystitis)Pyelonephritis (upper)
SiteBladderKidney
PainDysuria, suprapubicLoin/back, renal angle tenderness
SystemicUsually noneFever, rigors, nausea/vomiting
RiskDiscomfort, ascentSepsis, kidney scarring
📷 Image placeholder — Ascending urinary tract infection: bowel flora ascend the urethra → bladder (lower UTI / cystitis) → ureters → kidney (upper UTI / pyelonephritis), showing the anatomical basis of the lower-vs-upper fork
Uncomplicated vs complicated: pregnancy, men, catheter, structural abnormality, or immunosuppression all make a UTI complicated -- change duration and workup
Risk Factors & Aetiology
Risk Factors
  • Female -- shorter urethra; ~50% experience one in their lifetime
  • Pregnancy and post-menopause
  • New sexual activity (younger women)
  • Catheter / instrumentation
  • Stasis/obstruction: renal stones, urinary retention, BPH
  • Diabetes / immunosuppression
Organisms -- KEEPS
  • Bowel flora ascending the urethra -- the main mechanism
  • E. coli = commonest (gram-negative rod, faecal origin)
  • Klebsiella
  • Enterococcus
  • Proteus / Pseudomonas -- Proteus splits urea (urease) -- alkaline urine -- struvite stones
  • Staph saprophyticus -- classic in young sexually active women
  • Candida if fungal/catheter-related
Clinical Features
Lower UTI
  • Dysuria (burning on urination)
  • Suprapubic pain / tenderness
  • Frequency, urgency, incontinence
  • Haematuria
  • Cloudy, foul-smelling urine
Pyelonephritis (adds)
  • Fever, rigors
  • Loin / back pain
  • Renal angle tenderness (costovertebral angle)
  • Nausea, vomiting
  • Systemically unwell / septic
Elderly / frail: confusion may be the only feature. Always dip the urine in new-onset delirium -- but don't over-diagnose; asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in this group
Investigations
Uncomplicated lower UTI in women aged ≤65: diagnosis can be clinical with ≥2 of -- dysuria, urgency/frequency, absence of vaginal discharge

Urine dipstick (NICE decision logic):

Dipstick resultAction
Nitrites onlyTreat as UTI + send MC&S (gram-negatives convert nitrate to nitrite -- fairly specific)
Leucocytes + haematuriaTreat as UTI
Leucocytes onlyDo not treat as UTI
📷 Image placeholder — Urine dipstick decision logic: nitrites (± leucocytes) → treat + send MC&S; leucocytes + haematuria → treat; leucocytes alone → do not treat; do not dipstick over-65s or catheterised patients
MC&S (midstream urine)
  • Not needed for all uncomplicated cases
  • Essential in: pregnancy, recurrent UTI, atypical features, not improving on treatment
If pyelonephritis / septic
  • FBC, CRP, U&E
  • Blood cultures
  • VBG (lactate)
  • Renal USS -- exclude obstruction
Do not routinely dipstick patients over 65 or catheterised patients -- asymptomatic bacteriuria is common; dipstick misleads. Diagnose on symptoms.
Management
First-line Antibiotics
  • Nitrofurantoin -- 1st choice; avoid if eGFR <45 (needs renal concentration to work; toxicity risk)
  • Trimethoprim -- 2nd choice; high local resistance rates
  • Alternatives: pivmecillinam, amoxicillin, cefalexin
  • IV antibiotics if pyelonephritis, then step down to oral
Duration
  • Women, simple lower UTI -- 3 days
  • Men, pregnant, catheter-related -- 7 days
  • Immunosuppressed, abnormal anatomy, impaired renal function -- 5-10 days
Pre-treatment culture ideally. High fluid intake. Catheter UTI -- only treat if symptomatic AND replace the catheter.
Management in Pregnancy
Why it matters: UTI in pregnancy can cause pyelonephritis, premature rupture of membranes, and pre-term labour
  • All pregnant women with UTI -- send MSU and give 7 days antibiotics
  • Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy -- screened for and treated (unlike non-pregnant patients)

Antibiotic timing traps:

DrugCautionReason
TrimethoprimAvoid 1st trimesterFolate antagonist -- neural tube defects
NitrofurantoinAvoid 3rd trimesterNeonatal haemolysis
AmoxicillinOnly once sensitivities knownHigh resistance if empirical
CefalexinGenerally safeOften the pragmatic first choice in pregnancy
⭐ Exam Pearls
Lower vs upper
Lower = dysuria + suprapubic. Upper (pyelonephritis) = fever + loin pain + renal angle tenderness + systemic upset
KEEPS organisms
Klebsiella, E. coli (commonest), Enterococcus, Proteus/Pseudomonas, Staph saprophyticus
Proteus = struvite stones
Urease-splitting organism -- alkaline urine -- struvite (infection) stones. Proteus in urine = look for stones
Staph saprophyticus
Classic UTI in young sexually active women. The "not E. coli" UTI in that demographic
Elderly = confusion
Confusion may be the only feature of UTI in frail/elderly patients. Always dip in new delirium -- but don't over-diagnose asymptomatic bacteriuria
Dipstick logic
Nitrites alone = treat. Leucocytes + haematuria = treat. Leucocytes alone = do not treat
Nitrofurantoin avoid eGFR <45
Needs to concentrate in urine to work. Below eGFR 45 it's ineffective and toxic
Duration rules
Women = 3 days. Men / pregnant / catheter = 7 days
Pregnancy: treat asymptomatic bacteriuria
Unlike non-pregnant patients -- asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is screened for and always treated
Trimethoprim -- 1st trimester
Folate antagonist -- avoid in 1st trimester (neural tube defects)
Nitrofurantoin -- 3rd trimester
Avoid in 3rd trimester -- neonatal haemolysis
Recurrent / pyelonephritis
Renal USS to exclude obstruction (stone, BPH). Blood cultures if systemically unwell
UROLOGY__Renal Stone Disease:
Overview

Hard stones forming in the kidneys (nephrolithiasis) or ureters (urolithiasis) from supersaturation of urine causing crystal precipitation. Stone type drives radiology, cause, and prevention.

Two emergencies:
1. Obstruction -- AKI
2. Infection behind obstruction -- obstructive pyelonephritis (pus under pressure -- decompress urgently)
Three narrow points where stones lodge: Pelviureteric junction (PUJ) -- Pelvic brim (crossing iliac vessels) -- Vesicoureteric junction (VUJ)
📷 Image placeholder — Three ureteric narrowing points where stones lodge: pelviureteric junction (PUJ), pelvic brim where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels, and vesicoureteric junction (VUJ)
Stone Types
StoneFrequencyRadiologyKey association
Calcium (oxalate +/- phosphate) 80% Radio-opaque (visible on XR) Hypercalciuria / hypercalcaemia; oxalate-rich diet
Struvite (Mg-ammonium-phosphate) Radio-opaque Urease-producing UTI (Proteus, Klebsiella) -- forms staghorn calculi
Urate Radiolucent -- NOT on XR Hyperuricaemia / gout, ileostomy
Cystine Faintly opaque Cystinuria (autosomal recessive)
Radiology rule: Most stones radio-opaque on XR. Urate = radiolucent (XR-invisible). All stones visible on CT -- why CT KUB is the gold standard.
📷 Image placeholder — Stone types and radiology: calcium and struvite radio-opaque (visible on X-ray), urate radiolucent (X-ray-invisible), cystine faintly opaque — all visible on CT KUB
Calcium Stones (80%) -- Metabolic Causes
Hypercalcaemia
  • Calcium supplementation
  • Primary hyperparathyroidism -- most important to exclude
  • Malignancy
  • Tetrad: stones, bones, abdominal groans, psychiatric moans
Hyperoxaluria
  • Oxalate-rich diet (spinach, rhubarb, tea, beetroot)
  • Paradox: low dietary calcium -- less gut oxalate binding -- more absorbed -- more stones
  • Malabsorption / enteric causes
  • Primary (autosomal recessive)
Other causes
  • Medullary sponge kidney, polycystic kidney disease
  • Renal tubular acidosis (alkaline urine -- calcium phosphate stones)
  • Idiopathic hypercalciuria
Drug SBA -- the diuretic split
  • Thiazides PREVENT calcium stones -- increase distal tubular calcium reabsorption -- less calcium in urine
  • Loop diuretics PROMOTE calcium stones (also steroids, acetazolamide, theophylline)
Other Stone Types
Urate stones
  • Hyperuricaemia / gout
  • Ileostomy -- bicarbonate loss -- acidic urine -- uric acid precipitates
  • Radiolucent -- invisible on plain XR; seen on CT only
Struvite stones
  • Urease-producing organisms (Proteus, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas)
  • Urea -- ammonia -- alkaline urine -- precipitation
  • Form large staghorn calculi (cast of renal pelvis, "deer antler")
Cystine stones
  • Cystinuria -- autosomal recessive defect in renal tubular + GI transport of cystine and dibasic amino acids
  • Cystine (least soluble amino acid) precipitates in urine
  • Faintly radio-opaque; recurrent stones from childhood
Clinical Features
Often asymptomatic until a stone obstructs
Renal Colic
  • Unilateral, sudden, severe
  • Loin to groin radiation (flank -- pelvis -- testicle/labia)
  • Colicky -- waxes and wanes as stone moves
  • Patient cannot lie still (writhes) -- contrast with peritonitis (lies still)
  • Nausea, vomiting, haematuria
  • Reduced urine output if obstructed
Red flags / differentials
  • Always exclude ruptured AAA in older patients with flank/back pain -- can mimic colic exactly
  • Fever + flank pain = pyelonephritis until proven otherwise
  • Other differentials: biliary colic, bowel obstruction, lower-lobe pneumonia, MSK
Investigations
Imaging
  • Non-contrast CT KUB = gold standard -- detects all stone types including radiolucent urate; done within 24h of presentation
  • AXR -- shows calcium/struvite stones; misses urate (radiolucent)
  • USS KUB -- preferred in pregnancy and children (no radiation); less sensitive
Bloods + Urine
  • Urine dipstick: haematuria in most; screen for infection. Normal dip does NOT exclude a stone
  • FBC, CRP (infection), U&E (renal function)
  • Serum calcium (exclude hypercalcaemia)
  • Urate, PTH (if calcium stones, to exclude hyperparathyroidism)
  • Blood cultures if septic
Acute Management
1
Analgesia
NSAIDs = most effective (IM diclofenac preferred); IV paracetamol if NSAID CI
+
2
Antiemetic + fluids
Metoclopramide / cyclizine; IV fluids if dehydrated
then
3
Watchful waiting
Most stones <5 mm pass spontaneously, especially if distal ureter; consider an alpha-blocker (tamsulosin) as medical expulsive therapy for distal ureteric stones ≤10 mm (NICE)
if
!
Obstructed + infected
URGENT decompression -- ureteric stent (retrograde) or nephrostomy (antegrade)
Infected + obstructed kidney = decompress urgently. Antibiotics alone won't clear pus under pressure. Stent or nephrostomy first.
Definitive Stone-Clearing Procedures

For stones >10 mm, won't pass, complete obstruction, or infection:

ProcedureBest forNotes
ESWL (shock wave lithotripsy) Smaller stones <2 cm External shockwaves under XR guidance. CI: pregnancy, stone over bony landmark
Ureteroscopy + laser Ureteric stones Scope via urethra to ureter. Preferred in pregnancy (no radiation)
PCNL (percutaneous nephrolithotomy) Large renal stones / staghorn GA, scope via flank incision directly into kidney
Open surgery Rare Last resort
Recurrence Prevention
General (all stone types)
  • Fluids 2.5-3 L/day -- dilutes urine
  • Fresh lemon juice -- citrate binds urinary calcium
  • Avoid cola -- phosphoric acid promotes oxalate stones
  • Reduce salt intake
  • Maintain normal calcium intake -- do NOT restrict; low calcium worsens oxalate stones
Type-specific
  • Oxalate: reduce spinach, beetroot, nuts, rhubarb; potassium citrate; thiazide diuretics if hypercalciuria
  • Urate: reduce purines (offal, sardines, anchovies); allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor)
  • Calcium: check PTH (exclude primary hyperparathyroidism); limit animal protein
⭐ Exam Pearls
80% calcium
Calcium oxalate/phosphate = most common. Driven by hypercalciuria, hypercalcaemia, or hyperoxaluria
Urate = radiolucent
XR-invisible. CT KUB sees all stones -- that's why it's gold standard. AXR misses urate
Struvite = staghorn
Urease-producing organisms (Proteus) -- alkaline urine -- staghorn calculi (cast of renal pelvis)
Cystine = AR cystinuria
Autosomal recessive tubular transport defect. Recurrent stones from childhood
Loin to groin, can't lie still
Unilateral colicky pain. Patient writhes (vs peritonitis = lies still). The restlessness discriminates
Always exclude ruptured AAA
In any older patient with severe flank/back pain -- ruptured AAA mimics renal colic exactly and is immediately life-threatening
NSAIDs = best analgesia
IM diclofenac preferred. More effective than opioids for renal colic
<5 mm = watchful waiting
Most pass spontaneously especially if distal. >10 mm / obstruction / infection = intervene
Infected + obstructed = decompress
Ureteric stent (retrograde) or nephrostomy (antegrade) -- urgently. Antibiotics alone won't clear pus under pressure
ESWL vs PCNL vs ureteroscopy
ESWL <2 cm (not pregnancy). PCNL for staghorn/large renal. Ureteroscopy for ureteric / preferred in pregnancy
Thiazides PREVENT calcium stones
Increase distal tubular calcium reabsorption -- less in urine. Loop diuretics / steroids / acetazolamide PROMOTE them
Low calcium diet worsens oxalate stones
Paradox: less gut calcium means less oxalate binding -- more oxalate absorbed -- more stones. Maintain normal calcium intake
Hypercalcaemia tetrad
Stones, bones, abdominal groans, psychiatric moans. Always check serum calcium + PTH in calcium stone formers
USS in pregnancy/children
No radiation. Less sensitive but safe. CT KUB for everyone else
UROLOGY__Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (B:
Overview

Hyperplasia of the stromal and epithelial cells of the prostate causing bladder outflow obstruction. Affects men over 50 and presents with lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS).

Prostate Zone -- the BPH vs Cancer distinction
  • BPH = transitional zone -- surrounds the urethra; hyperplasia compresses urethra early and causes LUTS
  • Cancer = peripheral zone -- palpable on DRE, presents late (no urethral compression until advanced)
📷 Image placeholder — Prostate zonal anatomy: transitional (periurethral) zone — enlarges in BPH, compressing the urethra early; peripheral zone — where most prostate cancers arise, palpable on DRE
Risk Factors
  • Age (the main driver -- nearly universal by age 80)
  • Family history
  • African/Caribbean ethnicity
  • Obesity
Main complication: high-pressure chronic retention -- post-renal AKI. Always check renal function and look for hydronephrosis.
Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms (LUTS)
Voiding (obstructive) symptoms
  • Hesitancy -- difficulty initiating flow
  • Weak / poor stream
  • Intermittency -- flow stops and starts
  • Straining to void
  • Terminal dribbling
  • Incomplete emptying
Storage (irritative) symptoms
  • Urgency
  • Frequency
  • Nocturia
  • Urge incontinence
Why the split matters: Voiding symptoms -- alpha-blocker / 5-ARI (treat the obstruction). Storage symptoms -- bladder retraining / antimuscarinics (treat overactive bladder). Classification picks the drug.

IPSS scoring: 0-7 mild (watchful waiting), 8-19 moderate, 20+ severe (consider surgery)

Investigations

Digital rectal examination (DRE) -- key bedside test:

BPH (benign)Prostate cancer
SurfaceSmoothCraggy / irregular
SymmetrySymmetricalAsymmetrical
ConsistencyRubbery / slightly softFirm / hard
Central sulcusMaintainedLost
📷 Image placeholder — Digital rectal examination: BPH — smooth, symmetrical, rubbery, central sulcus maintained; prostate cancer — hard, irregular/craggy, asymmetrical, sulcus lost
PSA
  • Used to investigate for prostate cancer but poor specificity
  • Causes of raised PSA: prostate cancer, BPH, prostatitis, UTI, vigorous exercise, recent ejaculation, DRE itself
  • Counsel patients: avoid ejaculation and vigorous exercise for 48h before PSA test; do PSA before DRE
  • Finasteride halves PSA -- double the measured value to interpret correctly
Other
  • Urine dipstick -- infection, haematuria
  • Urine frequency-volume chart (3 days)
  • U&E -- renal function (obstruction damage)
  • Renal USS -- prostate size + check for hydronephrosis
  • Bladder scan -- post-void residual volume
Management

Watchful waiting for mild symptoms (IPSS <8). Lifestyle: reduce evening fluids, caffeine, alcohol.

Medical management:

DrugMechanismOnsetKey side effects
Alpha-1 antagonist
(tamsulosin, alfuzosin)		 Relaxes bladder neck + prostate smooth muscle -- rapid symptom relief Fast (days) Postural hypotension, dizziness, nasal congestion, retrograde ejaculation
5-alpha reductase inhibitor
(finasteride, dutasteride)		 Blocks testosterone -- DHT -- shrinks prostate over time Slow (up to 6 months) ED, reduced libido, ejaculation problems, gynaecomastia; halves PSA
Combination: tamsulosin (fast relief) + finasteride (long-term shrinkage) -- often used together in larger prostates

Storage symptoms / overactive bladder: bladder retraining (first-line) -- antimuscarinics (oxybutynin, tolterodine, darifenacin), or mirabegron (beta-3 agonist -- useful where antimuscarinic anticholinergic burden is a concern) if persistent

Surgical Management
For moderate-severe symptoms (IPSS ≥20), failed medical therapy, or complications (retention, AKI, recurrent UTI)
TURP (Transurethral Resection) -- commonest
  • Diathermy loop via urethral resectoscope -- resects prostatic tissue
  • Complications: haemorrhage, infection, incontinence, ED
  • Retrograde ejaculation -- the classic post-TURP complaint (semen goes into bladder)
  • Urethral stricture (late)
  • TURP syndrome -- see below
Other Procedures
  • HoLEP (holmium laser enucleation) -- larger prostates; less bleeding
  • TEVAP/TUVP (electrovaporisation) -- alternative to TURP
  • Open prostatectomy -- very large glands (>100g)
TURP syndrome: absorption of glycine irrigation fluid -- fluid overload + dilutional hyponatraemia
Features: confusion, nausea, agitation, visual changes, seizures -- life-threatening. Treat: fluid restriction, hypertonic saline if severe.
⭐ Exam Pearls
BPH = transitional zone
Surrounds the urethra -- obstructs early. Cancer = peripheral zone -- palpable on DRE, presents late
LUTS split
Voiding (hesitancy, weak flow, dribbling) -- treat obstruction (alpha-blocker / 5-ARI). Storage (urgency, frequency, nocturia) -- treat OAB (retraining / antimuscarinics)
DRE: BPH vs cancer
BPH = smooth, symmetrical, rubbery, sulcus maintained. Cancer = hard, irregular, asymmetrical, sulcus lost
PSA poor specificity
Raised by: cancer, BPH, prostatitis, UTI, vigorous exercise, ejaculation, DRE itself. Counsel before testing
Finasteride halves PSA
Double the measured PSA to interpret correctly in patients on finasteride. A "normal" level may mask cancer
Tamsulosin = fast
Alpha-blocker; symptom relief in days. SE: postural hypotension (warn about standing up quickly)
Finasteride = slow
5-ARI; shrinks prostate over up to 6 months. SE: ED, reduced libido, gynaecomastia. Only works in large prostates
Storage symptoms -- antimuscarinics
Bladder retraining first; then oxybutynin / tolterodine / darifenacin. Caution in men with high post-void residual -- may cause acute retention
TURP = commonest surgery
Retrograde ejaculation is the expected post-op complication -- warn patients pre-op. Semen refluxes into bladder
TURP syndrome
Fluid overload + dilutional hyponatraemia from absorbed irrigation fluid. Confusion + visual changes post-TURP = think TURP syndrome
Main complication
High-pressure chronic retention -- post-renal AKI. Always check U&E and USS for hydronephrosis in retention
UROLOGY__Prostate Cancer:
Overview

Commonest cancer in men. Most are slow-growing -- many die with it, not of it. Advanced disease spreads to lymph nodes and bone. Driven by androgens (testosterone/DHT) -- the basis of all hormonal treatment.

Anatomy -- the BPH contrast
  • Cancer = peripheral zone (75%) -- palpable on DRE; obstructs urethra late; explains silent early disease
  • BPH = transitional zone -- surrounds urethra; obstructs early; causes LUTS
  • >95% are adenocarcinoma; often multifocal
  • Ductal subtype: faster growing and metastasises more rapidly
Risk Factors
  • Increasing age (most important)
  • Family history
  • Black African / Caribbean ethnicity
  • BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations
  • Anabolic steroids, tall stature
  • Modifiable: smoking, diabetes, obesity
Clinical Features
Often asymptomatic -- peripheral zone tumours don't compress the urethra early; the key reason for late presentation
Localised
  • LUTS: hesitancy, weak flow, frequency, nocturia, dribbling, urgency
  • Often none
Advanced / Metastatic
  • Haematuria, dysuria, erectile dysfunction
  • Bone pain (osteoblastic mets -- axial skeleton)
  • Weight loss, lethargy
  • Cauda equina syndrome -- spinal cord compression (emergency)

DRE findings -- the three-way distinction:

Findings
BPHSmooth, symmetrical, rubbery, central sulcus maintained
ProstatitisEnlarged, tender, warm
CancerFirm/hard, asymmetrical, craggy, sulcus lost, +/- hard nodule
Any cancer-suspicious DRE -- 2-week-wait urology referral
PSA

PSA = glycoprotein from prostatic epithelium. Prostate-specific but not cancer-specific.

Unreliable: ~75% false positives, ~15% false negatives. Patients choose whether to test (shared decision -- not a screening programme).
Causes of raised PSA (non-cancer)
  • BPH, prostatitis (wait 1 month before testing), UTI
  • Vigorous exercise, recent ejaculation / prostate stimulation (wait 48h)
  • DRE itself -- do PSA before DRE
  • Finasteride halves PSA -- double the measured value to interpret correctly
Investigations

Multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) = first-line for suspected localised cancer (abnormal DRE or raised PSA). Reported on the Likert scale:

LikertMeaningAction
1-2Low suspicionSurveillance / reassurance
3EquivocalDiscuss biopsy with patient
4Probable cancerBiopsy
5Definite cancerBiopsy
Biopsy (if Likert ≥3)
  • Transperineal (through perineum) -- preferred; lower infection risk
  • TRUS (transrectal ultrasound-guided) -- higher infection risk
  • Risks: pain, bleeding, infection, retention, ED
Gleason Grading (histology)
  • Two most common architectural patterns scored 1-5 each, then added
  • 6 = low risk; 7 = intermediate; 8+ = high risk
  • 3+4 is better prognosis than 4+3 -- the dominant pattern matters
📷 Image placeholder — Gleason grading / ISUP Grade Groups: the two commonest histological patterns (each 1–5) added — 3+3=6 low risk (GG1), 3+4=7 (GG2) vs 4+3=7 (GG3), 8–10 high risk (GG4–5); the dominant pattern drives prognosis
Risk Stratification
RiskPSAGleasonStage
Low<10≤6T1-T2a

High>208-10≥T2c
Staging
  • Isotope bone scan -- mets take up more isotope; bone mets are osteoblastic (sclerotic) -- contrast with most lytic mets
    • 📷 Image placeholder — Prostate cancer bone metastases: osteoblastic (sclerotic/dense white) lesions in the axial skeleton on X-ray and increased tracer uptake on isotope bone scan — contrast with the lytic mets of most other cancers
  • CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for lymph node mets
  • PSMA PET-CT (modern staging)
Management
Management driven by risk stratification + life expectancy

Active surveillance vs watchful waiting -- the confused pair:

Active surveillanceWatchful waiting
ForCurable low-risk disease (younger, fit)Older / lower life expectancy
IntentCurative -- treat if progressesPalliative -- avoid treatment harms
Monitoring3-monthly PSA, 6-12 monthly DRE, rebiopsy 1-3 yrlySymptom-based only
Curative (localised disease)
  • Radical prostatectomy (prostate + seminal vesicles +/- pelvic nodes)
    SE: ED, stress incontinence, bladder neck stenosis
  • External beam radiotherapy
    SE: proctitis (pain, rectal bleeding, altered bowel habit) -- treat with prednisolone suppositories
  • Brachytherapy (I-125 seeds implanted transperineally)
    SE: cystitis, proctitis, ED, incontinence, secondary bladder/rectal cancer (late)
Advanced / Metastatic
  • Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) -- mainstay
  • GnRH agonists (goserelin, leuprorelin): cause initial tumour flare (bone pain, obstruction) -- pre-cover with anti-androgen (bicalutamide) first
  • Androgen receptor blockers: bicalutamide
  • Androgen-receptor pathway inhibitors (enzalutamide, abiraterone) — now added upfront to ADT in metastatic hormone-sensitive disease, not just at castrate-resistance
  • ADT SEs: hot flushes, sexual dysfunction, gynaecomastia, fatigue, osteoporosis
  • Chemotherapy (metastatic): docetaxel, cabazitaxel
⭐ Exam Pearls
Commonest male cancer
Androgen-driven. Peripheral zone -- silent early, palpable on DRE. BPH = transitional zone -- obstructs early
DRE: cancer = hard + craggy
Firm/hard, asymmetrical, craggy, sulcus lost, +/- nodule. Any suspicious DRE -- 2-week-wait referral
PSA unreliable
75% false positive. Raised by BPH, prostatitis, UTI, exercise, ejaculation, DRE. Do PSA before DRE
Finasteride halves PSA
Double the measured value to interpret. A "normal" PSA on finasteride may mask significant cancer
mpMRI first-line -- Likert score
Likert 1-2 = low suspicion. 3 = equivocal. 4-5 = probable/definite cancer -- biopsy
Transperineal biopsy preferred
Lower infection risk than transrectal (TRUS). Standard of care in most UK centres
Gleason grading
Two patterns added. 6 = low risk. 7 = intermediate (3+4 better than 4+3). 8+ = high risk
Active surveillance vs watchful waiting
AS = curative intent, low-risk younger men, 3-monthly PSA + rebiopsy. WW = palliative intent, older/comorbid, symptom-based only
Radical prostatectomy SEs
ED + stress urinary incontinence. Warn pre-op -- both are expected and common
Radiotherapy SEs
Proctitis (pain, rectal bleeding) -- treat with prednisolone suppositories. Brachytherapy also risks secondary malignancy (late)
GnRH agonist tumour flare
Initial surge in testosterone before castration -- can worsen bone pain and obstruction. Pre-cover with bicalutamide (anti-androgen) first
ADT side effects
Hot flushes, ED, gynaecomastia, fatigue, osteoporosis. Long-term ADT -- DEXA scan + bisphosphonates
Bone mets = osteoblastic
Sclerotic (not lytic) on XR. Isotope bone scan: mets take up more tracer. Cauda equina from spinal mets = emergency
UROLOGY__Bladder Cancer:
Overview

Cancer arising from the bladder lining. Most present as non-muscle-invasive (superficial) disease — this single distinction drives all management decisions.

Non-Muscle-Invasive (NMIBC)Muscle-Invasive (MIBC)
StageTis, Ta, T1T2–T4 / N+ / M+
TreatmentTURBT ± intravesical therapyRadical cystectomy ± chemo
PrognosisGood (but high recurrence)Worse
Risk Factors
Main Risk Factors
  • Smoking — #1 modifiable risk factor
  • Increasing age
  • Aromatic amines — dye/rubber industries (also in cigarette smoke) → urothelial carcinoma
  • Schistosomiasis → squamous cell carcinoma (endemic countries)
  • Pelvic radiotherapy
Classic Vignette

Retired dye-factory worker presenting with painless haematuria → think bladder cancer (aromatic amine exposure).

Types & Classification

Histological subtypes:

Type%Key Association
Urothelial (transitional cell)90%Smoking, aromatic amines — the default
Squamous cell carcinoma5%Schistosomiasis
Adenocarcinoma / sarcoma / small-cellRare—

StageExtentCategory
TisCarcinoma in situ — flat, urothelium onlyNMIBC
TaPapillary, urothelium onlyNMIBC
T1Into lamina propria — NOT into muscleNMIBC
T2–T4Into detrusor muscle and beyondMIBC

Painless visible haematuria = bladder cancer until proven otherwise — the single most important presenting symptom.
Common Symptoms
  • Painless visible haematuria — cardinal feature
  • Recurrent UTIs
  • LUTS — frequency, urgency, incomplete voiding
Advanced Disease
  • Locally advanced — pelvic pain
  • Metastatic — weight loss, lethargy

Commonest kidney tumour — an adenocarcinoma arising from renal tubules (cortex, mainly PCT, upper pole). The decisive exam topics: the classic triad, the paraneoplastic syndromes, and the two signature metastases (cannonball lung + left varicocele).

Overview

Twisting of the spermatic cord with rotation of the testicle. A urological emergency — delay causes ischaemia and necrosis, leading to sub-fertility or infertility. Typical patient: a teenage boy.

Diagnosis is clinical. If torsion is suspected, get immediate senior urology input and proceed to theatre. Negative imaging never overrides clinical suspicion.

Collection of fluid within the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis. Painless, soft scrotal swelling — testis palpable within it. Transilluminates.

Communicating (Infants)

Varicocele

Second-line for stress incontinence if surgery declined/unsuitable
Refractory urge — botox
Botulinum toxin A into bladder wall; sacral nerve stimulation
UROLOGY__Pyelonephritis:
Overview

Bacterial infection of the renal pelvis and parenchyma — the upper-tract UTI. Defined by the systemic triad on top of lower-UTI symptoms — that triad is what separates it from cystitis and signals the sepsis/scarring risk.

Lower UTI (Cystitis)Upper UTI (Pyelonephritis)
Dysuria, frequency, suprapubic painLower-UTI symptoms + fever + loin pain + nausea/vomiting
Local symptoms onlySystemic upset — sepsis risk
Risk Factors & Causes
Risk Factors
  • Female sex
  • Structural urological abnormalities
  • Vesico-ureteric reflux (VUR) — especially children
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Obstruction/stasis — stones, catheter, pregnancy
Causative Organisms
  • E. coli — commonest (gut flora ascending)
  • Klebsiella pneumoniae
  • Enterococcus
  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa
  • Staphylococcus saprophyticus
  • Candida albicans (fungal)
Clinical Features

Lower-UTI symptoms (dysuria, frequency, suprapubic discomfort) plus the upper-tract triad:

The defining triad:
1. Fever
2. Loin / back pain (uni- or bilateral)
3. Nausea / vomiting
  • Systemic illness, loss of appetite, haematuria
  • Renal angle (costovertebral) tenderness on examination

  • 3 treatments: O₂ to 94–98% (88–92% in COPD), IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, IV fluids
Not responding or symptoms severe? Think:

2. Obstructing stone — infected + obstructed kidney needs urgent decompression, not just antibiotics (cross-ref renal calculi)

Recurrent kidney infections → scarring of the renal parenchyma → chronic kidney disease → end-stage renal failure.

DMSA scan: radiolabelled DMSA accumulates in healthy kidney tissue. Areas that don't take it up on gamma-camera imaging indicate scarring/damage — used to assess renal damage in recurrent pyelonephritis.

UROLOGY__Bladder & Urodynamics:
A bladder scan is a portable, non-invasive ultrasound device that measures bladder volume at the bedside — most often the post-void residual (PVR), the volume left in the bladder immediately after the patient has voided. It is used to assess incomplete emptying, detect urinary retention and guide the decision to catheterise, all without the discomfort and infection risk of passing a catheter.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

The device fires ultrasound across the pelvis, automatically detects the bladder outline over several planes and reconstructs a 3D volume estimate in millilitres — a quick, operator-light approximation rather than a formal ultrasound study. Its great strength is that it avoids unnecessary catheterisation: a normal residual reassures without any instrumentation.

🔬Incomplete emptying
Suspected in LUTS, BPH, neurogenic bladder or recurrent UTI
🚻Retention
Acute (painful, sudden) or chronic (painless, high-volume)
💧Post-catheter check
Confirm bladder empties after a trial without catheter (TWOC)
📉Fluid balance
Distinguish anuria from obstruction in the oliguric patient
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

The patient lies supine. Ultrasound gel is applied to the lower abdomen and the probe is placed suprapubically, midline, angled slightly caudally toward the pelvis. The operator selects the correct sex setting (so the device does not mistake the uterus for bladder) and triggers the scan; the machine displays the estimated volume in seconds.

For a true PVR, scan immediately after voiding — ideally within 5–10 minutes, as the kidneys keep filling the bladder and delay inflates the reading.
No preparation, contrast, catheter or radiation is required — it is entirely non-invasive and repeatable.
Re-aim and re-scan a few times; take the highest consistent volume to reduce under-reading from a mis-angled probe.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the urological image / trace / specimen (e.g. the bladder-scanner screen showing the outlined bladder over the suprapubic probe with a numeric volume in mL).
3INTERPRETATION

PVR is interpreted against volume thresholds, always in the clinical context (symptoms, renal function, recurrent infection).

PVR <50 mL→Normal, complete emptying — no action
PVR 100–200 mL→Elevated / significant incomplete emptying — monitor, repeat, correlate with symptoms
PVR >300–500 mL→Large residual / retention — consider catheterisation
PVR >~1 L (painless)→Chronic retention (may be high-pressure) — catheterise and check U&Es for obstructive nephropathy
Near-zero after TWOC→Successful trial without catheter — bladder emptying restored
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY

The scanner gives an estimate, not a measured volume, and several situations make it read falsely high.

Over-reads with ascites, ovarian or renal cysts, and large bladder diverticula — the device counts non-bladder fluid as urine.
Obesity and lower-abdominal scars/staples scatter the beam and reduce accuracy.
The gravid uterus, fibroids or recent pelvic surgery can confuse the outline; a delayed scan inflates a genuine PVR.
Painful, tender, palpable bladder + high scan volume→Acute retention — catheterise for symptom relief
🚩 A bladder scan is a screening estimate, not a diagnosis — never withhold catheterisation in a patient with painful acute retention or rising creatinine from suspected obstruction just because the number looks modest; treat the patient, and remember ascites or a cyst can fabricate a large "residual".
🎓 High-yield: for an accurate PVR, scan within minutes of voiding — a full PVR done late overestimates residual because the kidneys refill the bladder (~1–2 mL/min). Normal PVR is <50 mL; persistently >100 mL warrants review.

Uroflowmetry is a simple, non-invasive urodynamic screening test in which the patient voids a comfortably full bladder into a rotating-disc or weight-transducer flowmeter, producing a flow-rate-versus-time curve. Its headline output is Qmax (the maximum urinary flow rate, mL/s), supported by voided volume, average flow, and the shape of the trace. It is a first-line objective test for lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) — particularly suspected bladder outflow obstruction from benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) — but it detects only that flow is low, not why.

1Indication & principle

Flow rate is the net result of the detrusor pushing against outlet resistance. A low, prolonged flow can arise either from a high-resistance outlet (obstruction) or from a weak pump (detrusor underactivity) — uroflowmetry alone cannot separate the two.

🚹BPH / BOO
Male LUTS, hesitancy, poor stream — screen for outflow obstruction
🩹Urethral stricture
Classic flat, plateau (box-shaped) low-flow curve
📉Weak detrusor
Underactive bladder producing an equally low flow
🔁Treatment monitoring
Objective before/after outcome for TURP or drugs
2How it is performed
Patient attends with a comfortably (not painfully) full bladder and voids privately into the flowmeter funnel in the normal standing or sitting position.
A voided volume ≥150 mL is required for the trace to be valid; smaller volumes artificially depress Qmax and give unreliable results.
The device records voided volume, Qmax, average flow (Qave), time to Qmax, and flow time, and plots the curve.
Ideally repeat on ≥2 occasions, and pair with a bladder scan for post-void residual (PVR) volume.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the urological image / trace / specimen (e.g. a normal bell-shaped uroflow curve beside an obstructed low-plateau trace with annotated Qmax).
3Interpretation

Read the peak value and the shape together, always in the context of an adequate voided volume.

Qmax >15 mL/s→Broadly normal flow; obstruction unlikely
Qmax 10–15 mL/s→Equivocal — interpret with symptoms and PVR
Qmax <10 mL/s→Suggests bladder outflow obstruction OR weak detrusor
Smooth bell-shaped curve→Normal voiding pattern
Flat plateau (box) curve→Urethral stricture / fixed outflow resistance
Intermittent / interrupted curve→Straining or abdominal voiding, often with underactive detrusor
4Pitfalls, limitations & safety
Volume dependence: a void <150 mL invalidates the study and is the commonest cause of a spuriously low Qmax.
Cannot localise the cause: low flow does not distinguish obstruction from detrusor underactivity — invasive pressure-flow studies (measuring detrusor pressure at peak flow) are needed to prove obstruction.
Artefacts: straining, wobble of the funnel, cruising the stream around the cone, and self-consciousness in an unnatural setting all distort the trace.
🚩 Do not treat a single low Qmax as diagnostic of obstruction — if the voided volume is inadequate or a decision to intervene (e.g. TURP) hinges on the cause, confirm with a pressure-flow study, as operating on an underactive bladder mistaken for obstruction gives poor results.
🎓 A flat, low, box-shaped plateau curve is the exam signature of a urethral stricture, whereas BPH classically gives a low, prolonged curve with a delayed, reduced peak — but only a pressure-flow study confirms true obstruction.

Pressure-flow urodynamics (cystometry) is the reference-standard, invasive test of lower-urinary-tract function. Fine catheters simultaneously measure intravesical (bladder) pressure (Pves) and abdominal pressure (Pabd, via a rectal balloon); the clinically useful detrusor pressure is derived electronically as Pdet = Pves − Pabd. The bladder is filled to reproduce symptoms and then the patient voids, so the study characterises the storage phase (overactivity, compliance, capacity, sensation) and the voiding phase (contractility and outflow resistance) — distinguishing bladder outflow obstruction from detrusor underactivity when non-invasive tests are equivocal.

1Indication & principle

Because urodynamics is invasive, it is reserved for situations where non-invasive assessment (symptoms, flow rate, post-void residual, diary) cannot explain the picture or where the wrong operation would harm the patient. The core principle is subtraction: only by removing abdominal (straining) pressure from bladder pressure can a true detrusor contraction be identified.

🔬Equivocal male LUTS
Confirm obstruction before prostate surgery (TURP/HoLEP) when the diagnosis is unclear, e.g. borderline flow or suspected underactivity
🧠Neurogenic bladder
Spinal cord injury, spina bifida, MS — assess storage pressures and detect high-pressure storage that threatens the upper tracts
💧Refractory OAB
Confirm detrusor overactivity before botulinum toxin or before considering major storage surgery
🔁Failed prior surgery
Persistent or complex incontinence after previous continence/prostate surgery before re-intervention
2How it is performed

The patient attends with a comfortably full bladder; free (non-invasive) uroflowmetry and a post-void residual are recorded first. A double-lumen catheter is passed transurethrally to fill the bladder and read Pves, and a fluid-filled or air-charged balloon catheter is placed in the rectum (or vagina/stoma) to read Pabd. Both transducers are zeroed to atmosphere at the level of the pubic symphysis and Pdet is derived by subtraction.

Cough test — the patient coughs periodically; equal spikes on Pves and Pabd (flat Pdet) confirm both lines are transmitting pressure correctly.
Filling phase — sterile saline (often room temperature) is instilled at a medium rate (~10–50 mL/min); first sensation, first desire, strong desire and cystometric capacity are logged.
Provocation — coughing, running water and postural change are used to provoke leakage or unstable contractions.
Voiding phase — the patient voids around the catheter into a flowmeter so Pdet and flow are recorded simultaneously (the pressure-flow plot).
📷 Image placeholder — annotated urodynamic trace showing paired Pves, Pabd and derived Pdet channels with the synchronous flow curve during the voiding phase.
3Interpretation, cut-offs & grading

The diagnosis is read from the two phases together: the storage trace shows overactivity and compliance, and the synchronous pressure-flow plot separates obstruction from underactivity.

High Pdet + low Qmax during voiding→Bladder outflow OBSTRUCTION (bladder generates pressure but cannot empty)
Confirmed BPH outflow obstruction→alpha-blocker (tamsulosin) → add a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (finasteride) if the prostate is large (works over months) → TURP if refractory
Low Pdet + low Qmax during voiding→Detrusor UNDERACTIVITY (weak contraction — TURP unlikely to help)
Underactive detrusor or repeatedly failed TWOC→CISC (clean intermittent self-catheterisation) or a long-term catheter, with urology follow-up — outflow surgery will not help a weak detrusor
Phasic involuntary Pdet rises during filling→Detrusor OVERACTIVITY (correlates with urgency ± urgency incontinence)
Bladder Outlet Obstruction Index (PdetQmax − 2×Qmax) > 40→Obstructed (20–40 equivocal, < 20 unobstructed) in men
Gradual pressure climb with no volume plateau, loss of accommodation→Poor compliance — sustained end-fill Pdet ≥ 40 cmH₂O threatens the upper tracts
Leakage on cough with a flat Pdet (abdominal pressure only)→Urodynamic stress incontinence, not detrusor overactivity
Confirmed stress incontinence→pelvic floor muscle training first line, then duloxetine or surgery (colposuspension / mid-urethral sling)
4Pitfalls, limitations & safety
Artefact from poor subtraction — a dislodged, blocked or air-bubble-filled rectal line makes Pdet uninterpretable; regular cough tests are mandatory to verify the trace.
Non-physiological setting — voiding to order around a catheter in a lab may not reproduce home symptoms, and up to a quarter of men fail to void; a single normal study does not exclude intermittent overactivity.
Catheter effect — the filling catheter itself can partially obstruct flow and lower measured Qmax relative to free flow.
🚩 Urodynamics is invasive instrumentation of the urinary tract and carries a risk of UTI and, rarely, urosepsis. Screen and treat symptomatic infection before the study, use aseptic technique, and give prophylactic antibiotics for high-risk patients (e.g. neurogenic bladder, recurrent UTI, immunosuppression) — warn patients to seek help for fever or rigors afterwards.
🎓 The whole point of the rectal line is subtraction: a true detrusor contraction raises Pves while Pabd stays flat, so Pdet rises. Straining raises Pves and Pabd equally, leaving Pdet unchanged — this is exactly how urodynamics separates genuine detrusor overactivity from abdominal straining and how it distinguishes obstruction from a weak detrusor.

A bladder diary (frequency-volume chart, FVC) is a patient-completed paper or app record kept over ≥3 consecutive days that logs fluid intake, the time and volume of every void, and any urgency or incontinence episodes. It is the first-line, objective, non-invasive assessment of lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) — it converts a vague history ("I go all the time") into hard numbers on functional bladder capacity, total and nocturnal urine output, and voiding frequency, and it directs conservative management before any invasive urodynamic testing.

1Indication & principle

Requested for anyone with troublesome LUTS — storage symptoms (frequency, urgency, nocturia, incontinence) or voiding symptoms — where the history alone cannot separate causes. NICE recommends it as a core, low-cost first step. The principle is simple: measured output over time reveals patterns the patient cannot report accurately from memory, distinguishing a bladder problem from an output (renal/fluid) problem.

💧Overactive bladder
urgency with small frequent voids
🌙Nocturia / nocturnal polyuria
excess night-time urine output
🚰Global polyuria
high 24-h volume ≥40 mL/kg
🥤Excess/irritant intake
caffeine, alcohol, high fluids
2How it is performed

The patient is given a chart and a measuring jug and asked to record, for at least 3 (ideally not necessarily consecutive but representative) days including typical work and rest days:

Time and volume of every void (mL), day and night.
Fluid intake — time, type and volume of drinks.
Urgency episodes and any incontinence / leakage events (and pad use).
Time to bed and time of waking, to define the night-time period.

No catheter, probe, radiation or contrast is involved — the only equipment is a jug and a chart, making it cheap and fully non-invasive. Accuracy depends entirely on patient compliance, so clear instruction is essential.

📷 Image placeholder — describe the urological image / trace / specimen (e.g. a completed 3-day frequency-volume chart showing columns for time, intake, voided volume and urgency/leakage, with a tall cluster of night-time voids).
3Interpretation — the key numbers

Derive: functional bladder capacity (the largest single voided volume), total 24-h output, nocturnal urine volume (night voids plus the first morning void), and daytime/night-time frequency.

Nocturnal volume >33% of 24-h output (older adult)→Nocturnal polyuria
24-h output ≥40 mL/kg body weight→Global polyuria (consider diabetes, primary polydipsia, DI)
Small frequent voids + urgency, normal 24-h output→Overactive bladder / reduced functional capacity
High total intake & output, large voids→Excess fluid intake — treat with fluid advice
Maximum voided volume markedly reduced→Low functional capacity — storage disorder or fibrotic bladder

In young adults the nocturnal threshold is higher (>20% of output); the >33% cut-off applies to older patients. These derived values steer diagnosis without a single needle or scan.

4Pitfalls, limitations & use in management

The chart is only as good as the patient's diligence — incomplete or estimated entries make it uninterpretable, and a single atypical day can mislead, hence the ≥3-day minimum. It quantifies but does not explain mechanism: it cannot measure detrusor pressure, flow rate or post-void residual, so a chart suggesting outflow obstruction or detrusor overactivity may still need uroflowmetry, bladder scan or formal urodynamics. It also cannot exclude UTI, so dysuria or haematuria warrant urinalysis first.

Nocturnal polyuria identified→Evening fluid/caffeine/alcohol restriction, review diuretic timing
Overactive bladder pattern→Bladder training & caffeine reduction, then antimuscarinic / mirabegron
🚩 A bladder diary is an assessment tool, not a diagnosis. Persistent visible haematuria, suspected UTI, or output patterns suggesting undiagnosed diabetes mellitus or diabetes insipidus must be investigated in their own right — never attribute polyuria to "drinking too much" without excluding these before starting bladder training.
🎓 The single most useful number an examiner will ask for is the largest voided volume = functional bladder capacity, and the definition of nocturnal polyuria = night-time urine >33% of the 24-h total in older adults (nocturnal volume includes the first morning void but excludes the last void before bed).

A Trial Without Catheter (TWOC) is a planned removal of an indwelling urethral catheter to test whether a patient can void spontaneously after a period of catheterisation — most often following an episode of acute urinary retention (AUR). It is not itself an imaging or pressure study but a functional bedside test of lower urinary tract emptying, judged on whether the patient passes urine adequately and on the post-void residual (PVR) measured by bladder scan. Success means the catheter can stay out; failure means re-catheterisation and urology follow-up.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

TWOC is offered once the precipitant of retention has been treated and the bladder has had time to recover from over-distension. The principle is simple: an over-stretched or transiently obstructed detrusor may regain effective contractility after a period of decompression, so a controlled trial identifies who no longer needs a catheter.

🔬Post-AUR (BPH)
Commonest — men catheterised for retention from benign prostatic enlargement
💊Reversible cause
Constipation, UTI, drugs or post-op retention — treat first, then trial
🩺Post-procedure
After catheter placed for surgery or short-term drainage
In men with retention secondary to BPH, starting an alpha-blocker (e.g. tamsulosin) for at least 24–48 h before TWOC relaxes prostatic and bladder-neck smooth muscle and significantly improves the chance of successful voiding.
A first episode of AUR with a modest drained volume and treated precipitant is a good candidate; very high drained volumes or chronic retention warrant more caution.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

TWOC is typically scheduled in the morning (community TWOC clinic or ward) so any failure can be managed in working hours.

Preparation: ensure the precipitant is treated, the patient is well hydrated, and (in men with BPH) an alpha-blocker has been started. Confirm no active UTI requiring treatment first.
Remove the catheter: deflate the balloon fully and withdraw. Encourage normal fluid intake and ask the patient to void when they feel the urge.
Monitor voids: record each voided volume and symptoms over the next few hours.
Measure PVR: perform a portable bladder scan immediately after voiding to quantify the residual urine — this is the objective measure of bladder emptying.
📷 Image placeholder — describe the urological image / trace / specimen (e.g. a portable bladder-scanner display showing the calculated post-void residual volume in mL).
3INTERPRETATION

Success is a clinical judgement combining adequate spontaneous voiding with an acceptably low PVR and the absence of distressing symptoms.

Voids good volumes + low PVR (e.g. <100–200 mL)→Successful TWOC — catheter stays out, arrange follow-up
Unable to void / painful distended bladder→Failed TWOC — re-catheterise and refer to urology
Voids small amounts but high residual PVR→Incomplete emptying — failed trial, re-catheterise
Failed first TWOC in BPH→Continue alpha-blocker, consider repeat TWOC or long-term catheter pending surgery
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
Re-retention: voiding once does not guarantee sustained emptying — the patient can re-obstruct hours later, so give clear safety-netting on when to return.
Post-obstructive diuresis: after relief of chronic (high-volume) retention the kidneys can pass large urine volumes, risking dehydration and electrolyte disturbance — monitor urine output, fluid balance and U&Es.
Untreated UTI: trialling with an active infection risks failure and sepsis; treat first.
PVR cut-offs are not absolute: a modestly raised residual in a comfortable, well-voiding patient may still be acceptable — interpret alongside symptoms and volumes.
🚩 After relieving chronic high-volume retention beware post-obstructive diuresis — monitor urine output, fluid balance and renal function, and watch for re-retention even after an apparently successful void.
🎓 In men with retention from BPH, prescribe an alpha-blocker (tamsulosin) at least 24–48 hours before the TWOC — this measurably increases the chance of a successful trial and is a classic exam point.
UROLOGY__Cancer Imaging & Biopsy:
Transurethral resection of bladder tumour (TURBT) is an endoscopic operation performed via a rigid resectoscope passed per urethra, in which a papillary or sessile bladder tumour is resected in fragments using a diathermy loop. It is simultaneously therapeutic (it removes all visible tumour) and diagnostic/staging (it yields tissue to determine tumour grade — low vs high — and, most importantly, the depth of invasion, i.e. whether the muscularis propria/detrusor is involved). This single question — muscle invaded or not — separates non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC: Ta, T1, CIS) from muscle-invasive disease (MIBC, ≥T2) and dictates the entire treatment pathway.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

TURBT is indicated for any suspicious bladder lesion seen on cystoscopy or imaging, typically in a patient investigated for visible (macroscopic) haematuria. The principle is to resect the exophytic tumour down to and including a bite of underlying detrusor muscle, so the pathologist can assess grade and stage in one specimen.

🩸Visible haematuria
Commonest presenting trigger for cystoscopy and subsequent TURBT.
🔬Tissue diagnosis
Provides histological grade and T-stage to guide management.
✂️Tumour removal
Complete resection of all visible NMIBC is often curative.
📊Muscle sampling
Detrusor must be in the specimen for adequate staging.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Performed under general or spinal anaesthesia with the patient in lithotomy. A rigid resectoscope is passed transurethrally and the bladder inspected in full (an examination under anaesthesia, EUA, is done to assess a palpable mass and fixation). The tumour is resected in layers with a monopolar or bipolar diathermy loop; irrigation fluid distends the bladder and clears debris. The base is separately biopsied to obtain muscularis propria (detrusor). Haemostasis is achieved by coagulation and a three-way catheter is left for irrigation.

Exophytic tumour and its stalk/base are resected and sent as separate specimens where possible.
A deep bite of detrusor is taken from the tumour base to enable staging.
Photodynamic (blue-light) cystoscopy or narrow-band imaging may improve detection of CIS and small lesions.
3INTERPRETATION — GRADE & STAGE

Histology reports two things: grade (WHO low-grade vs high-grade urothelial carcinoma) and T-stage (depth of invasion). The pivotal line is between non-muscle-invasive (Ta/T1/CIS) and muscle-invasive (≥T2) disease.

Ta — non-invasive papillary→NMIBC; confined to urothelium
CIS (Tis) — flat high-grade→NMIBC but aggressive; intravesical BCG
T1 — invades lamina propria→NMIBC, higher risk; re-resect if high-grade
Ta/T1 non-muscle-invasive→Intravesical therapy (mitomycin/BCG) + cystoscopic surveillance
T2 — invades muscularis propria→Muscle-invasive: radical cystectomy or radical chemoradiotherapy
No detrusor in specimen→Understaged — repeat TURBT required
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
Understaging if no muscle is sampled — the single commonest quality failure; mandates re-resection.
Bladder perforation (usually extraperitoneal, managed with prolonged catheter drainage; intraperitoneal perforation may need repair).
Obturator kick — stimulation of the obturator nerve on lateral wall resection causes sudden leg adduction and risks perforation.
Post-operative haematuria and clot retention, and risk of UTI/urosepsis after instrumentation.
Sampling error in a bulky tumour may miss a focus of deeper invasion.
🚩 Beware bladder perforation and significant post-op haematuria/clot retention. For suspected NMIBC, give a single immediate post-operative intravesical dose of mitomycin C (within 24 h) to reduce recurrence — but withhold it if perforation is suspected or bleeding is heavy, as extravasation of the cytotoxic agent can cause severe tissue damage.
🎓 High-yield: a high-grade T1 tumour (or any specimen lacking detrusor) warrants a re-resection (second-look TURBT) within 2–6 weeks — a substantial proportion are upstaged to muscle-invasive disease on repeat resection, changing management entirely.

A CT KUB (non-contrast CT of the Kidneys, Ureters and Bladder) is the first-line imaging investigation for suspected acute renal or ureteric colic. Performed without any contrast, it detects virtually all urinary calculi — including radiolucent uric-acid stones that are invisible on plain film — and defines their exact size and location. It also demonstrates the secondary signs of obstruction (hydronephrosis, hydroureter, perinephric stranding), guiding whether a stone will pass spontaneously or needs urological intervention.

1Indication & principle

Indicated for acute loin-to-groin pain with suspected ureteric colic, and for characterising stone burden before planned intervention. The principle is a rapid, thin-slice helical CT acquired without contrast: calcium- and non-calcium calculi are markedly denser than surrounding soft tissue, so nearly all stones appear bright regardless of chemical composition. Sensitivity and specificity both exceed 95%, making it the reference standard.

🔬Radiolucent stones
Uric-acid & xanthine stones missed on X-ray are still seen on CT
⚡Speed
Scan acquired in seconds — ideal for the acutely painful patient
🚫No contrast
Avoids contrast nephrotoxicity & allergy; no cannula prep needed
📈Accuracy
>95% sensitivity & specificity — the diagnostic gold standard
2How it is performed

Minimal preparation is required. The patient lies supine (occasionally prone to distinguish a distal ureteric stone from one already passed into the bladder). A single helical acquisition covers the top of the kidneys to the base of the bladder in one breath-hold. No oral or IV contrast is given, and no bowel prep or fasting is needed.

Thin (1–3 mm) contiguous slices are reconstructed in axial, coronal and sagittal planes to trace the ureter.
The whole tract is followed from renal pelvis to vesico-ureteric junction to localise the stone.
Attenuation is measured in Hounsfield units (HU), hinting at stone composition and treatment response.
3Interpretation

Report the stone's size, site and density, plus any signs of obstruction. Stone size is the key driver of management.

Stone <5 mm→High chance of spontaneous passage — conservative management with analgesia & hydration
Stone 5–10 mm→Consider medical expulsive therapy (alpha-blocker e.g. tamsulosin) ± intervention
Stone >10 mm→Unlikely to pass — urological intervention (ureteroscopy, ESWL or PCNL)
Hydronephrosis / hydroureter proximal to stone→Confirms obstruction — monitor renal function & urgency of treatment
Perinephric fat stranding & rim sign→Supports an acutely obstructing calculus rather than a phlebolith
Density >1000 HU→Suggests hard calcium-oxalate monohydrate — more resistant to ESWL
Density ∼300–500 HU→Suggests uric-acid stone — may respond to urinary alkalinisation
4Pitfalls, limitations & safety
Radiation: delivers an ionising dose; low-dose CT KUB protocols are used in slim patients and for follow-up to minimise exposure.
Pregnancy: CT is avoided — ultrasound is the first-line investigation in pregnant women to prevent fetal radiation.
Mimics: pelvic phleboliths can be mistaken for distal ureteric stones; use the comet-tail and soft-tissue rim signs to differentiate.
Non-opaque exception: pure indinavir (protease-inhibitor) stones are the rare calculi that may not be visible even on CT.
No functional data: a non-contrast scan shows anatomy only — it does not assess split renal function or excretion.
🚩 An obstructing stone with signs of infection or sepsis (fever, rigors, raised inflammatory markers, an obstructed infected system) is a urological emergency. It requires urgent decompression by nephrostomy or ureteric stent plus IV antibiotics — delay risks pyonephrosis, irreversible renal loss and death.
🎓 A stone missed on plain KUB X-ray but causing classic colic is very likely a radiolucent uric-acid stone — CT KUB will reveal it, and its lower Hounsfield density flags a stone amenable to dissolution by urinary alkalinisation.

A CT urogram (CTU) is a multiphase, contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis that adds a delayed excretory (urographic) phase to opacify the pelvicalyceal systems, ureters and bladder with excreted iodinated contrast. It is the first-line upper-tract imaging test for visible (macroscopic) haematuria and the key investigation for suspected upper-tract urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma (TCC), demonstrating filling defects, urothelial thickening and enhancing masses that flow cytology and plain imaging miss.

1Indication & principle

Visible haematuria in an adult mandates urgent (2-week-wait) investigation of the whole urinary tract. Because urothelium lines the tract from calyces to urethra, TCC can arise anywhere — so the pathway pairs upper-tract cross-sectional imaging with direct bladder inspection.

CT urogram assesses the kidneys, collecting systems and ureters (upper tract).
Flexible cystoscopy assesses the bladder and urethra (lower tract) — CTU is not sensitive enough for small bladder tumours.
Principle: iodinated contrast is filtered and excreted, so a delayed phase fills the lumen and outlines any intraluminal lesion as a filling defect.
🔬Upper-tract TCC
Filling defect / enhancing mass in renal pelvis, calyx or ureter
🩸Visible haematuria
Any age — commonest reason to request a CTU
🪨Stone / obstruction
Anatomy of a dilated or obstructed system
🧭Anatomy mapping
Duplex systems, strictures, surgical planning
2How it is performed

The patient is well hydrated and cannulated; renal function (eGFR) is checked before intravenous iodinated contrast. A standard protocol acquires images in timed phases after the contrast bolus:

Unenhanced phase — detects calcification and calculi (which enhance would obscure).
Nephrographic phase (~90–100 s) — renal parenchyma enhances uniformly; best for detecting enhancing renal and urothelial masses.
Excretory / urographic phase (~7–15 min) — contrast fills the calyces, pelvis and ureters, outlining filling defects and urothelial thickening.

Adjuncts such as low-dose IV furosemide, oral hydration and prone or delayed imaging improve distension and opacification of the whole ureter.

3Interpretation

Interpretation combines the enhancing nephrographic images with the opacified excretory phase. Findings are matched to meaning:

Filling defect in pelvis / calyx / ureter→Upper-tract TCC until proven otherwise (differentials: clot, non-opaque stone)
Enhancing soft-tissue lesion that enhances on nephrographic phase→Tumour rather than clot (clot does not enhance)
Focal urothelial thickening / mural enhancement→Early / flat urothelial malignancy or inflammation
Hydronephrosis / hydroureter to a lesion→Obstructing tumour or stricture; assess level and cause
Non-enhancing, mobile, dependent defect→Blood clot — reassess after treatment rather than assume tumour
Dense, high-attenuation defect on unenhanced phase→Calculus — the unenhanced phase distinguishes stone from tumour

Local T-staging notes perinephric or periureteric fat stranding and invasion; nodal and metastatic disease are assessed on the same study. A suspicious upper-tract lesion is confirmed with ureteroscopy and biopsy, and staged for management.

4Pitfalls, limitations & safety
Radiation dose is significant (multiple phases) — justify and dose-optimise, especially in younger patients.
Poor opacification / distension can hide small ureteric lesions; suboptimal excretory phase is a common cause of a false-negative study.
Clot vs tumour — a non-enhancing defect may be clot; enhancement and interval reimaging help.
Not for the bladder — CTU under-detects small bladder tumours, so cystoscopy remains mandatory in haematuria.
eGFR reduced / diabetic on metformin→Assess contrast risk; hydrate; follow local metformin and renal protocols
🚩 Intravenous iodinated contrast can cause contrast-induced nephropathy and, rarely, anaphylactoid reactions. Always check renal function (eGFR) and contrast-allergy history before scanning; in significant renal impairment or prior severe reaction, weigh benefit against harm and consider an alternative (e.g. MR urogram or retrograde studies) with senior input.
🎓 In visible haematuria the answer is both: CT urogram for the upper tract and flexible cystoscopy for the bladder — neither alone clears the whole urothelium. A filling defect that enhances is tumour; a filling defect that does not enhance is likely clot or a non-opaque stone.

Multiparametric MRI of the prostate (mpMRI) combines T2-weighted anatomy, diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI/ADC) and dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) sequences to detect and localise clinically significant prostate cancer. It is now performed before biopsy so that suspicious lesions can be targeted and men with reassuring scans can safely avoid biopsy. Findings are reported on the PI-RADS scale of 1–5, the likelihood of clinically significant disease, and the scan also stages local spread (extracapsular extension, seminal vesicle invasion).

1Indication & principle

mpMRI is indicated in men with a raised PSA and/or abnormal digital rectal examination where prostate cancer is suspected, as the first-line investigation ahead of any biopsy. Each sequence interrogates a different tissue property, and cancer characteristically restricts water diffusion and shows early avid enhancement.

🧲T2-weighted
Anatomy & zones; cancer is low-signal in the high-signal peripheral zone. Dominant for staging.
💧DWI / ADC
Restricted diffusion (high DWI, low ADC) — the dominant sequence for peripheral-zone tumours.
🩸DCE
Gadolinium contrast; early focal enhancement. Tie-breaker that upgrades an equivocal peripheral-zone lesion.
🎯Zone-dependent
DWI leads in the peripheral zone; T2 leads in the transition zone.
2How it is performed

Ideally the scan is done at least 6–8 weeks after any prostate biopsy so post-biopsy haemorrhage does not mimic or mask tumour. Imaging uses a 1.5T or 3T magnet with a pelvic phased-array coil; an antispasmodic (e.g. hyoscine butylbromide) may be given to reduce bowel motion artefact. Intravenous gadolinium is administered for the DCE sequence, so renal function and contrast allergy are checked first.

No routine bowel prep or endorectal coil needed on modern scanners.
Sequences are read together (multiparametric), not in isolation.
A structured PI-RADS report gives an overall score plus lesion location and size.
3Interpretation: PI-RADS & staging

PI-RADS v2.1 grades the likelihood of clinically significant cancer from 1 to 5 and drives the biopsy decision.

PI-RADS 1–2 (low)→Clinically significant cancer unlikely; biopsy may be safely avoided (shared decision, PSA follow-up)
PI-RADS 3 (equivocal)→Intermediate; individualise using PSA density — biopsy often offered
PI-RADS 4–5 (high)→Clinically significant cancer likely; MRI-targeted biopsy of the lesion
Bulging capsule / breach, neurovascular contact→Extracapsular extension (≥ T3a) — affects surgical planning
Low-T2 signal in seminal vesicles→Seminal vesicle invasion (T3b)

NICE supports an mpMRI-first pathway: a Likert/PI-RADS score of 3 or more prompts targeted biopsy, while a score of 1–2 allows biopsy to be omitted after discussing the small residual risk with the patient.

4Pitfalls, limitations & safety
Post-biopsy haemorrhage (T1-bright) can obscure or mimic tumour — scan before biopsy or delay after it.
Prostatitis, BPH nodules and haemorrhage cause false positives; some low-grade or cribriform cancers are MRI-invisible (false negatives).
Transition-zone tumours are harder to call and rely on T2 morphology.
Reporting is operator-dependent; quality needs adequate scanner and reader experience.
🚩 A normal (PI-RADS 1–2) mpMRI does not exclude cancer — roughly 1 in 10 clinically significant cancers is missed, so a rising PSA or highly suspicious DRE still warrants biopsy despite a reassuring scan. Gadolinium requires checking eGFR and allergy history before administration.
🎓 DWI/ADC is the dominant sequence for peripheral-zone lesions and T2 for transition-zone lesions; DCE mainly acts as a tie-breaker to upgrade an equivocal PI-RADS 3 peripheral-zone lesion to a 4.

Prostate biopsy is the tissue-sampling procedure that confirms and grades prostate cancer, converting a suspicion raised by a high PSA, an abnormal digital rectal exam (DRE) or a suspicious multiparametric MRI into a histological diagnosis. Cores are sampled either transrectally under ultrasound guidance (TRUS) or, increasingly in UK practice, transperineally to reduce infective risk. The pathologist assigns a Gleason score from the two commonest architectural patterns, which maps onto the ISUP Grade Group (1–5) that drives prognosis and management.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Biopsy is triggered when clinical or imaging findings suggest clinically significant prostate cancer. NICE recommends multiparametric MRI before biopsy so that suspicious lesions can be targeted and some men with low-suspicion scans can safely avoid biopsy.

🔬Raised PSA
Age-adjusted elevation prompting further assessment
✋Abnormal DRE
Nodule, asymmetry or hard craggy gland
🧲Suspicious MRI
PI-RADS/Likert 3–5 lesion to target
🔁Rising PSA
Prior negative biopsy with ongoing suspicion or active surveillance

The principle is simple: ultrasound (or MRI fusion) localises the gland and any target, and a spring-loaded needle removes thin cores of tissue for histological grading.

2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

The patient is counselled and consented; antiplatelet/anticoagulant status is checked. An ultrasound probe is placed in the rectum to image the prostate and guide the needle.

Transrectal (TRUS): needle passes through the rectal wall; quick, local anaesthetic, but higher infective risk from gut flora.
Transperineal: needle passes through perineal skin (prepped), sampling the gland without traversing bowel — markedly lower sepsis risk and now favoured in the UK.
MRI-targeted cores sample the suspicious lesion, usually combined with systematic cores across the gland to avoid missing untargeted disease.
Typically 10–12+ cores are taken; each is labelled by site and sent in formalin for histology.
3INTERPRETATION — GLEASON & ISUP GRADING

The Gleason system scores the two most common architectural patterns (each 3–5, well to poorly differentiated) and sums them, e.g. 3+4=7. The first number is the dominant pattern, so 3+4 behaves better than 4+3. Scores map to ISUP Grade Groups 1–5.

Gleason 6 (3+3)→ISUP GG1 — low grade, often suitable for active surveillance
Gleason 7 (3+4)→ISUP GG2 — favourable intermediate, dominant well-differentiated pattern
Gleason 7 (4+3)→ISUP GG3 — unfavourable intermediate, dominant poorly-differentiated pattern
Gleason 8 (4+4, 3+5, 5+3)→ISUP GG4 — high grade
Gleason 9–10→ISUP GG5 — highest grade, most aggressive

The report also states the number of positive cores, percentage core involvement and presence of perineural or extraprostatic spread, which together with PSA and stage feed risk stratification.

4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
Negative biopsy, persistently high PSA→Sampling error — cancer may be missed; consider repeat/targeted biopsy
Self-limiting haematuria / haematospermia→Expected; blood in urine and semen can persist for weeks — reassure
Fever, rigors, dysuria post-procedure→Suspect urosepsis — urgent assessment and antibiotics
Grading can be upgraded on the final surgical specimen, so biopsy Gleason is an estimate, not the whole gland.
Acute urinary retention and vasovagal episodes may occur around the procedure.
🚩 Post-biopsy sepsis is the key risk, especially with the transrectal route which crosses the rectal mucosa — give prophylactic antibiotics, and the transperineal approach substantially lowers infective risk. Any patient with fever or rigors after biopsy needs urgent review for urosepsis.
🎓 Remember the first Gleason digit is the dominant pattern: 3+4=7 (GG2) is prognostically better than 4+3=7 (GG3) despite the identical sum — a classic exam discriminator.

Scrotal ultrasound with colour Doppler is the first-line imaging test for the scrotum and testes, using a high-frequency (7.5–15 MHz) linear probe to characterise scrotal lumps and pain. Grey-scale imaging separates solid from cystic lesions and defines whether an abnormality is intra- or extra-testicular, while colour and spectral Doppler assess testicular perfusion — central to the assessment of the acute scrotum. It reliably diagnoses tumour, epididymo-orchitis, hydrocele and varicocele, but in suspected testicular torsion it must never delay surgical exploration.

1Indication & principle

Ultrasound is chosen because the testis is superficial and fluid/solid tissue reflect sound differently, giving excellent soft-tissue resolution without ionising radiation. Colour Doppler adds a functional layer — blood flow — which is the deciding factor in the acute scrotum. It is the go-to test for any palpable scrotal abnormality, pain, swelling, trauma or suspected malignancy.

🔬Scrotal lump
Solid vs cystic; intra- vs extra-testicular
🩸Acute scrotum
Assess flow — torsion vs infection
💧Swelling
Hydrocele, varicocele, epididymal cyst
🧪Raised markers
AFP/β-hCG/LDH prompting tumour search
2How it is performed

The patient lies supine with the scrotum supported on a towel and the penis retracted onto the abdomen; warm gel is applied. Both testes are scanned in longitudinal and transverse planes, comparing size, echotexture and flow side-to-side — the asymptomatic testis is the internal control. Colour and spectral Doppler settings are optimised for slow flow (low pulse-repetition frequency). Varicocele assessment includes standing and Valsalva to demonstrate venous reflux.

Grey-scale: size, echogenicity, focal lesions, tunica, epididymis.
Colour Doppler: presence and symmetry of intratesticular flow.
Spectral trace: arterial waveform and venous reflux with Valsalva.
3Interpretation

Pattern recognition links the grey-scale appearance and the Doppler flow to a diagnosis.

Solid intratesticular mass→Testicular tumour until proven otherwise — urgent referral, tumour markers, staging CT
Absent / markedly reduced testicular flow→Torsion — supports the diagnosis but does not replace exploration
Increased flow + enlarged tender epididymis→Epididymo-orchitis (hyperaemia)
Anechoic fluid surrounding testis, no flow→Hydrocele
Serpiginous veins >2–3 mm, reflux on Valsalva→Varicocele (usually left-sided)
Well-defined anechoic extratesticular lesion→Epididymal cyst / spermatocele — benign
4Pitfalls, limitations & safety

Doppler is operator- and settings-dependent: in early or intermittent (partial) torsion, or in a small prepubertal testis with low baseline flow, arterial signal may still be present — a normal-looking scan does NOT exclude torsion. Conversely, a large reactive hydrocele or marked oedema can obscure flow. Ultrasound cannot reliably distinguish benign from malignant solid lesions, so any solid intratesticular mass is treated as cancer until histology proves otherwise. Findings must always be read against the clinical picture and duration of symptoms.

🚩 Do NOT delay surgical exploration to obtain an ultrasound when torsion is clinically suspected — the testis is at risk of irreversible ischaemia after roughly 6 hours. Time is testis: explore first, image later.
🎓 A left varicocele that fails to empty when the patient lies flat, or a new right-sided varicocele, should prompt imaging of the abdomen/retroperitoneum for a mass obstructing venous drainage (e.g. renal tumour compressing the gonadal/renal vein).

PSMA PET-CT is a molecular imaging study that fuses positron-emission tomography with CT to map prostate cancer at the cellular level. A radiotracer (68Ga-PSMA-11 or 18F-DCFPyL) binds prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA), a transmembrane glycoprotein massively overexpressed on prostate adenocarcinoma cells. Sites of tracer avidity flag tumour, letting the scan stage high-risk disease and pinpoint recurrence at PSA levels far below the reach of CT or bone scintigraphy.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

PSMA is a folate-hydrolase enzyme expressed at low levels on benign prostate epithelium but upregulated 100–1000 fold on malignant cells, with expression rising as tumours dedifferentiate. A radiolabelled small-molecule ligand latches onto the extracellular PSMA domain and is internalised, concentrating the positron-emitter within cancer deposits. The fused CT provides the anatomical map for each avid focus.

🎯High-risk staging
Newly diagnosed high-risk / unfavourable-intermediate disease before radical treatment, to detect nodal or distant spread
📈Biochemical recurrence
Rising PSA after prostatectomy or radiotherapy with negative conventional imaging, to localise the relapse site
🔬Molecular target
PSMA overexpressed on prostate cancer cell membrane; ligand binds and is internalised
🧭Therapy guidance
Maps disease burden to direct salvage radiotherapy, nodal treatment or systemic therapy
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED
The radiotracer is injected intravenously; a 60-minute uptake period allows binding and background clearance before imaging.
No fasting or bowel prep is required; the patient voids before scanning as tracer is excreted renally and pools in the bladder.
A combined PET-CT scanner acquires the PET emission data and a low-dose (or contrast-enhanced) CT for anatomical co-registration, typically skull-base to mid-thigh.
Avidity is quantified by the standardised uptake value (SUV); intensity is often reported against liver and blood-pool reference using the PSMA-RADS or PROMISE frameworks.
3INTERPRETATION
Focal avidity in pelvic / retroperitoneal nodes→Nodal metastatic or recurrent disease — upstages, may divert from local-only therapy
Avid focus in bone without a CT lytic/sclerotic correlate→Early skeletal metastasis, detectable before bone scan turns positive
Avidity in prostate bed after prostatectomy→Local recurrence — target for salvage radiotherapy
Detection rate rises with PSA→~40–50% positive at PSA <0.5 ng/mL, climbing to ≥90% at PSA ≥2 ng/mL
No abnormal avidity→No PSMA-expressing macroscopic disease identified — does not exclude micrometastasis

Its high sensitivity for small-volume disease is the key advantage: PSMA PET-CT is markedly more accurate than combined CT plus bone scan for detecting nodal and distant metastases in high-risk staging, changing management in a substantial proportion of patients.

4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
Physiological uptake in salivary/lacrimal glands, liver, spleen, small bowel, kidneys and bladder is normal and must not be called disease.
PSMA is not prostate-specific: benign uptake occurs in coeliac/sympathetic ganglia (a classic node mimic), healing ribs and fractures, Paget disease, and some non-prostatic tumours and inflammatory nodes — causing false positives.
Poorly differentiated or neuroendocrine-dedifferentiated prostate cancer may lose PSMA expression, giving false negatives despite active disease.
It carries a radiation dose and is costly with limited availability; tracer supply (particularly 68Ga generator logistics) can constrain access.
🚩 A single PSMA-avid focus, especially in bone or a solitary node, can be a benign mimic (ganglion, fracture, Paget). Do not upstage a patient or deny curative treatment on one equivocal spot — correlate with CT morphology, PSA kinetics and, where it changes management, histological confirmation.
🎓 PSMA PET-CT is superior to CT plus bone scan for staging high-risk prostate cancer, and its sensitivity at low PSA makes it the go-to for biochemical recurrence when conventional imaging is blank. High-yield mimic to remember: symmetrical uptake in coeliac ganglia masquerading as retroperitoneal nodes.
